Q: How to SELECT rows from two tables which have a parent-child relationship and print the data in groups in a CodeIgniter view A:

Should check codeigniter active records and the join function. you can achieve it with the following query:

$query = $this->db->select("*")
    ->from('users')
    ->join('hobbies', 'user.id', '=', 'hobby.user_id')
    ->get()
    ->result_array();

you can now var_dump $query to check ur data and format it accordingly.

Q: Getting the Average of Rows Based on DateTimeIndex in Pandas A:

Did you check what you get in df.loc['begin':'end']['Number']?
It should give empty dataset because you have to use variables [begin:end]
instead of strings ['begin':'end']

print(begin, end)
print(df.loc[begin:end]["Number"])
print(df.loc[begin:end]["Number"].mean())

At this moment it calculates mean for one month + first day in next month.
If you want full month then you would have to substract one day from end.

end = pd.Timestamp("2008-02-01") + pd.DateOffset(months=num) - pd.DateOffset(days=1)

If you want to get mean() for every month in year then maybe you should groupby() using strings "year-month"

result = df.groupby(df.index.strftime("%Y-%m"))["Number"].mean()

rolling is for overlapping windows/subsets,
groupby is for non-overlapping windows/subsets.

It seems it allows to use MS,ME

result = df.groupby(pd.Grouper(freq="ME"))["Number"].mean()

result = df.groupby(pd.Grouper(freq="MS"))["Number"].mean()

python - Pandas groupby month and year - Stack Overflow

Full code for test - I added more rows in every month:

text = """
Date,Number
2008-01-01,5
2008-01-03,15
2008-02-01,55
2008-02-21,3
2008-03-01,6
2008-03-11,16
2008-04-01,10
2008-04-09,20
"""


import pandas as pd
from pandas.tseries.offsets import DateOffset
import io

df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(text))
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"])
df = df.set_index(["Date"])

print("--- df ---")
print(df)
# print(df.dtypes)

print("--- for-loop ---")
for num in range(0, 4):
    begin = pd.Timestamp("2008-01-01") + pd.DateOffset(months=num)
    end = pd.Timestamp("2008-02-01") + pd.DateOffset(months=num) - pd.DateOffset(days=1)
    # print(df.loc[begin:end]["Number"])
    print(begin, "|", end, "|", df.loc[begin:end]["Number"].mean())

print("--- groupby ---")
result = df.groupby(df.index.strftime("%Y.%m"))["Number"].mean()
print(result)

print("--- groupby 'ME'---")
result = df.groupby(pd.Grouper(freq="ME"))["Number"].mean()
print(result)

print("--- groupby 'MS'---")
result = df.groupby(pd.Grouper(freq="MS"))["Number"].mean()
print(result)

Q: What exactly is memory-mapped I/O and port-based I/O? A:

In port based io if I write to a port will it affect the corresponding memory address or not and vise versa.

No. A port is accessed with an in/out instruction, it doesn't have a "memory address" that the CPU can see.

mov dx,03C4h
mov al,02h
out dx,al

mov al, byte ptr [03C4h] ; this isn't going to make AL = 2 necessarily.

To make things even more confusing, a value written to a memory-mapped IO port doesn't always change the value at that address either! It's very common for certain IO ports to have different behavior on read vs. write.

For example, many game consoles have a memory-mapped IO port that can be read to tell you which row of pixels on is being drawn right now. But if you write to that address, it doesn't cause the video chip to start drawing at that line immediately. Rather, it tells it "I want an interrupt to occur at the Xth row of pixels" where X is the value written to the port. In other words, reading this address and writing to it represent two totally different things. C compilers don't really understand this as a concept and will try to optimize out behavior where you do something that would otherwise be pointless, like read from a memory address you just wrote to. Which is pointless for normal memory, but not for memory-mapped IO. The volatile keyword when applied to a variable prevents C from optimizing out reads or writes to it. This might relate to your question about caching, but I'm not sure exactly.

In order to know what will or won't happen, you need to be familiar with the platform you're working on. Most of them are well-documented, but every once in a while you'll have some ambiguous edge cases where you're not sure what will happen.

In memory mapped io there are some problems related to cache, what are those problems?

That I'm not entirely sure. I think there can be a problem where you try to read from one of these ports and since it's cached you're reading a previous value you didn't intend.

Q: Eclipse: navigate to method declaration in new editor? A:

Is there a way [...] to open that method declaration [...] in a new editor tab?

Starting with Eclipse 4.41 (Eclipse 2026-09), yes.

The Java editor now includes an Open in New Editor option in the hyperlink popup for types and methods.

See Open Types and Methods in a New Editor from Hyperlinks.

Open the hyperlink popup for the method or type, then select Open in New Editor.
That works when navigating to a declaration, implementation, or method in the same editor: the target opens in a separate editor tab without replacing your current location.

That means the previous workaround of first using Window > Editor > Clone is no longer necessary.

Also is there a way to navigate back to the previous place where your cursor was?

Use Navigate > Back (Alt+Left). You can return with Navigate > Forward (Alt+Right).

See Eclipse Platform Tips and Tricks: "Now, where was I?".

Q: Check out a branch without populating worktree? A:

Checkout is a convenience command to do some safety checks, load the index, set the HEAD reference and sync the work tree plus run any post-checkout hooks and such.

The stripped-down version you want isn't a common enough workflow to have its own convenience options, but you can use the core commands it relies on, this is one of the simplest examples like this:

git read-tree -m HEAD refs/heads/thatbranch &&
git update-ref   HEAD refs/heads/thatbranch

and the main difference between that and git checkout thatbranch is, it doesn't use read-tree's -u option to sync the work tree.

I found read-tree's docs a bit too inside-baseball for me so I made my own easier-for-me version of the table in its manpage.
